purpose: Conceptual illustrations of Bitwright's current implementation; exact circuits are in the native .circ files.

initialPrompts.prompt:
Use case: scientific-educational. Create a polished, visually interesting editorial illustration for Bitwright, a real gate-built computer simulated in Logisim. Landscape 3:2, high resolution, crisp typography. Consistent visual language: warm ivory paper, ink-navy fine linework, teal data paths, restrained amber clock/control accents, small green signal lights, subtle print grain; sophisticated 1970s engineering-manual meets modern isometric cutaway. Lots of breathing room, large readable labels, carefully composed depth. No photorealistic PCB or physical-product claims, no Apple logo, no mouse, no fake simulator screenshots. Conceptual explanatory art, not an exact wiring schematic. The native CPU is made of gates; do not portray a commercial CPU chip hiding the logic. Avoid random pseudo-text and decorative illegible labels.
Primary request: show the key components of Bitwright's actual CPU as an exploded isometric architecture map, with clearly labeled functional modules and a few elegant directed connections.
Title exactly: "BITWRIGHT"
Subtitle exactly: "Inside the gate-built CPU"
Central focus: an exposed layered module labeled "Alu6502", with tiny repeated full-adder/gate shapes visible under its surface, connected to a bank of five clearly distinct 8-bit register blocks labeled "A", "X", "Y", "SP", "P"; use one shared label "8-bit registers". A separate double-width register labeled "PC · 16-bit". Smaller input instruction register labeled "IR · 8-bit" leading into "InstructionDecode", then "Hardwired control". Decoder and control are explicitly gates, not ROM. Control connects to register enables and ALU with dashed amber lines, while main operand/result data paths are teal. Right side show an abstract interface split into "Address · 16-bit", "Data in · 8-bit", "Data out · 8-bit", attached to a simple memory silhouette labeled "Memory / I/O". Show address direction outward, data input inward, data output outward. A small clock waveform supplies the amber control layer.
Use a modest set of semantically meaningful routes rather than dense invented wiring. Include a slim explanatory caption: "8-bit data • 16-bit addresses • gate-built registers and control". Small footer exactly: "Conceptual view of Bitwright — not an original 6502 die layout". The architecture is functionally 6502-like, not an accurate chip die or physical implementation. Prioritize an inviting understandable visual over a dense schematic.

Primary request: a two-part exploded cutaway explaining how primitive gates become arithmetic and storage in Bitwright. Title exactly "BITWRIGHT / FROM GATES TO A COMPUTER". Two balanced zones, visually distinct but sharing one composition. Left heading "ARITHMETIC"; right heading "STATE".
LEFT: an eight-bit ripple-adder assembly built from exactly eight repeated full-adder cells, with carry moving sequentially along the chain. Label the group "8-bit ripple adder"; label a single expanded cell "FullAdder". An enlarged inset shows recognizable XOR, AND and OR logic symbols, without pretending the decorative wiring is a tested netlist. Show two operand ribbons labeled "A" and "B", sum ribbon labeled "SUM", and the small serial connection labeled "CARRY". A single short correct equation "SUM = A XOR B XOR Cin" is allowed inside the one-bit inset. Add caption "Used by add, subtract and compare".
RIGHT: an 8-bit register represented by exactly eight storage slices in a row labeled "Register8R0". A zoom callout expands ONE slice labeled "GateDff" into two transparent layers labeled "MASTER" and "SLAVE", containing cross-coupled gate motifs and feedback loops. Add short labels "Clock low" at master and "Clock high" at slave. Clock pulse lines in amber; stored bits in teal. Show a separate small latch for the whole bank labeled "Enable latch". Do not show built-in flip-flop symbols as the foundation: the gate structures must remain visibly exposed. The GateDff master/slave is a conceptual cutaway, not child GateLatch subcircuits.
Bottom small caption exactly "Primitive gates → reusable cells → inspectable CPU". Footer "Conceptual cutaways; native .circ files contain the exact circuits". Make it rich, elegant, tangible, and educational, not a generic block diagram.

Primary request: a visually engaging architecture journey through the complete actual Bitwright computer, carefully separating the host from circuit logic. Title "BITWRIGHT / FROM INPUT TO PIXELS". Wide horizontal visual narrative, beautiful vintage-engineering isometric cutaway with three clear zones marked "HOST INPUT", "CIRCUIT COMPUTER", "HOST DISPLAY".
At far left draw an ASCII keyboard and a small file sheet labeled ".mon". Both feed a host input module labeled "ASCII queue". A modest file callout says "Assembled program records". A dashed boundary leads into a gate-built module labeled "Keyboard latch"; then into an exposed gate CPU labeled "Gate-built 6502". Show circuit-owned "4 KiB RAM" and "Monitor ROM" alongside the CPU with clear memory connections. Place short annotation near input-to-CPU route: "Firmware parses records into RAM". ROM here is software only, never instruction control hardware.
From CPU show character output into a circuit terminal subsystem containing "Character RAM", "Cursor / scroll", "Font ROM" and "Pixel scan", with minimal sensible arrows: CPU characters to character RAM; cursor/scroll controls terminal layout; character RAM and font ROM feed pixel scan. This subsystem is labeled "40 × 24 text terminal". Then raw pixel output crosses the second dashed boundary into a period-inspired green display labeled "Raw pixel display". Screen text exactly "SUM (HEX) = 2D" above a small backslash prompt. The illustrated monitor is a visual metaphor for the Java pixel bridge, not analog circuitry.
Use two tiny captions at boundaries: "ASCII + acknowledge" and "Raw pixels". Bottom caption "Circuits execute the program and generate the text image." Small footer "Apple-1-inspired • Digital display • No host CPU emulation". All firmware execution, address decoding, character generation and scrolling occur within the central circuit zone. Host only provides ASCII capture/file queue and retained pixels. No mouse. No disk controller, no operating system, no network.

correctionPrompts.prompt: Edit this Bitwright architecture illustration, preserving its beautiful warm-paper engineering-manual style and overall composition. Correct the architecture routing specifically. The 16-bit PC must NOT join the 8-bit register data bus or feed the 8-bit Alu6502. Re-route PC to a new modest block labeled "Address generation / selection", then to the "Address · 16-bit" outgoing interface. Remove the false ALU-to-address connection. Keep the ALU and operand/result data paths explicitly 8-bit. Data-out selection is CPU interface logic, not only an ALU output; do not imply otherwise. P is the status register: label it "P · status" and connect it as flags/status feedback, not an ordinary operand register. Keep A X Y SP under the 8-bit-register heading, P is also 8-bit but status role distinct. Ensure instruction decoder and control look gate-built. Remove decorative corner slogans to create space for the address block; don't add new slogans. Preserve title, colors, fonts, conceptual-view footer and broad educational composition. No random labels. This is a simplified functional illustration, no exact netlist claim.

Edit this Bitwright artwork preserving its excellent overall style, title and two-column layout. Keep the eight adder cells and eight storage slices above. Correct misleading fake wiring in the two lower zoom panels by making them explicitly conceptual block cutaways instead of invented working schematics.
In the FullAdder inset replace the connected gate schematic with a single beautiful transparent one-bit cell, containing recognizable but UNCONNECTED XOR/AND/OR gate motifs. Three distinct input arrows A, B, Cin and two outputs SUM, Cout terminate at the cell boundary. Show the two correct equations beneath, with readable typography: "SUM = A XOR B XOR Cin" and "Cout = (A AND B) OR (Cin AND (A XOR B))". No extra input-to-input wire connections.
In the GateDff inset replace the fake network with two transparent boxes in series: D arrow → MASTER box → SLAVE box → Q arrow. Within each box draw a small abstract feedback-loop motif clearly representing stored state, not an exact gate netlist. Master label "Transparent when clock is low"; slave "Transparent when clock is high". An amber clock line splits to each box without being electrically joined to data, indicated functionally. Remove Q-bar output to keep simple. Add one tiny shared label "Conceptual cutaways" above these insets. Keep separate bank enable latch above and no invented detailed wiring around it; make it a labeled amber module controlling the register clock. Preserve footer saying native .circ files contain exact circuits. No additional slogans or pseudo-text.

Edit this Bitwright input-to-pixels architecture illustration. Preserve the excellent layout, colors, cutaway aesthetic and three host/circuit zones. Correct these factual labels and connections:
1. Remove "(Motorola S-record format)" completely. Replace the example text on the .mon file with exactly these three lines: "0300: A9 41 20 EF FF", "0305: 4C 03 FF", "0300R". These are Bitwright monitor deposit/run records, not S-records. Caption below file should only say "Assembled program records".
2. The CPU address bus label must read "Address bus (16 bits)", not 12 bits. Show a small gate block labeled "Address decode" before RAM and ROM, letting memory-chip address widths remain implicit.
3. Place "Firmware parses records into RAM" beside the CPU, not beside the keyboard latch. This is CPU firmware's job.
4. Remove "8 × 8 glyphs" under Font ROM; replace with "5 × 7 glyphs / 8 × 8 cells".
5. Replace "Generates 1-bit pixel stream..." with "Generates pixel output from character and font data." Do not claim exact interface width.
6. CPU-to-terminal must enter terminal control and character RAM; font ROM is read by pixel scan. Remove the apparent CPU data feed directly into Font ROM.
7. Add readable small note near memory modules: "RAM / ROM are allowed storage foundations". Change central subheading from all-gates-complete-computer claim to "Gate-built CPU and terminal logic". CPU remains gate-built; bulk RAM/ROM are simulator primitives.
Keep green screen "SUM (HEX) = 2D". No new claims, slogans, invented protocol names or labels. Keep all other essential structure.

finalCpuAtlasPrompt:
Edit the supplied Bitwright CPU illustration into a clean COMPONENT ATLAS, not a wiring diagram. Preserve its warm ivory, navy/teal/amber palette, isometric cutaway illustration quality and large BITWRIGHT title. Replace subtitle with "The CPU component atlas". Remove ALL connecting buses, wires and arrows BETWEEN the main modules so there can be no misleading data routes. Arrange six generous numbered exhibit areas in a balanced 3-by-2 layout on the paper. Each is an isometric illustrated object with a single concise label and caption. Use EXACTLY these labels/captions:
"01 / REGISTERS" — "A, X, Y, SP, P · 8-bit"; depict five short storage bars. P is the status register.
"02 / PROGRAM COUNTER" — "PC · 16-bit"; depict one double-width storage bar.
"03 / ARITHMETIC + LOGIC" — "Alu6502 · 8-bit"; depict an exposed tray of tiny logic-gate shapes. NO tiny operation list or additional text.
"04 / INSTRUCTION DECODE" — "IR and gate-built opcode decoding"; depict an instruction storage bar beside a gate network.
"05 / HARDWIRED CONTROL" — "State sequencing, enables, clock and reset"; depict a clock waveform and gate-based control block; no ROM.
"06 / MEMORY INTERFACE" — "16-bit addresses · 8-bit data in / out"; depict three separated connector ribbons that END locally inside this exhibit and do not connect to other exhibits.
Only these six groups, no duplicate components, no pseudo schematics, no bogus chip markings. Bottom caption "Built as inspectable gate circuits in Logisim". Footer "Conceptual component portraits — see native .circ files for exact connections". Remove original data-path legend and slogans. Preserve elegant proportions and readable typography.
